explanations.answer: The loving devotion of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The writer says, “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail.” After all that pain, he doesn't point to anything he built or earned. I think that's why hope can show up in the dark.

explanations.answer: The strength of the city walls
explanations.explanation: Walls are handy, friend, but the writer never reaches for them here. He says, “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed…” That's where he puts his hope. Stone doesn't even get a mention.

Nearby nations is a natural thought, but the writer names no help from them. He says it's “…the loving devotion of the LORD” that keeps us from being consumed. In this verse, the credit goes to the LORD alone.

I can see why you'd say that, since he's been saying “we” and “His.” But look at the next words: “…great is Your faithfulness!” That “Your” means he turns and speaks straight to the LORD. He stops talking about Him and starts talking to Him.

Right on. The word is “Your,” not “His,” so he's speaking straight to the LORD. Verse 22 talks about Him, and verse 23 turns and talks to Him. I think that's a man too full of hope to keep it in third person.
Yes sir. The soul says, “The LORD is my portion,” and then adds, “therefore I will hope in Him.” A portion is a share, friend, the piece that's yours. And the soul says that piece is the LORD.
Fortress sounds right, doesn't it? Strong, solid, stays put. But the soul uses a different word here: “The LORD is my portion…” It's a word about a share, and that's the one in this verse.
A banner is a flag, and it's a fun guess for a poem with such big feelings. This soul doesn't wave one, though. It says, “The LORD is my portion…” That's the word to hold onto.

Yes. The writer says, “The LORD is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him.” Waiting doesn't sound like much, friend, but he says it right out. He even calls it good to wait quietly in the very next verse.

If the list were only for people who never stumble, I'd have been turned away ages ago. I've face-planted into the chocolate chips on purpose and by accident. The writer names “those who wait for Him” and “the soul who seeks Him.” Stumbling never comes up.

Strength sounds like a natural pick, but the writer doesn't name the already strong. He says the LORD is good to “those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him.” Waiting and seeking are what he lists. Nobody's flexing in this verse.
That's it. The writer says, “Let him sit alone in silence, for the LORD has laid it upon him.” It's a heavy line, and I think it's worth sitting with. Notice who he names: the LORD.
No king shows up in this verse. The writer says, “…for the LORD has laid it upon him.” The one he names is the LORD. That's the word that fills the blank.
A priest is a fair guess, but no priest appears in this verse. The writer says the LORD has laid it upon him. That's the name in the blank. It's a hard line, and I think it's meant to be read slowly.
Yes. After the face in the dust comes the line “…perhaps there is still hope.” I think this one hurts to read. Then that little light shows up right behind it.
It's easy to read this verse and see only the dust. But the writer adds, “…perhaps there is still hope.” I think this verse hurts, and hope still shows up in it. So the statement is true.

explanations.answer: The Lord will not cast us off forever
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. After the dust and the cheek, he says, “For the Lord will not cast us off forever.” The heavy part doesn't get the last word. Verse 32 keeps going from there.

explanations.answer: The Lord will punish our enemies soon
explanations.explanation: Punishing enemies is a natural thought, but the writer doesn't say it here. His reason is “For the Lord will not cast us off forever.” That's the line that follows the dust and the cheek. Enemies don't get a mention.

explanations.answer: The Lord will rebuild the city walls
explanations.explanation: Rebuilt walls would be nice news, but the writer doesn't say it. His reason is “For the Lord will not cast us off forever.” Not a word about bricks. This verse is about us, not construction.

Yes sir. “Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion.” Grief is real in this poem, and the writer says so out loud. But compassion follows right in the same verse.

Anger would flip the verse upside down. The writer says, “…He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion.” Grief is named, yes, but compassion comes right after it. That one word is the whole turn.

Silence does show up earlier in the passage, when a man sits alone in silence (Lamentations 3:28), but it's not what He shows here. The verse says, “…He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion.” Compassion is the word that fits.

I can see why, with all that grief around, but the verse says the opposite. It says, “For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men.” So the statement is false. Hold onto that word “willingly.”

Right. The verse says, “For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men.” The writer just said grief can happen, and now he adds that it isn't something He does willingly. That's a lot of comfort in one little word.

Yes. He lists crushing prisoners underfoot, denying a man justice, and twisting a man's lawsuit. Then he says, “…of these the Lord does not approve.” Those are heavy things, friend. He doesn't hedge, he just says it.

The verse says the opposite. Right after the three things, the writer says, “…of these the Lord does not approve.” So the Lord does not approve of crushing prisoners, denying justice or twisting a lawsuit. Nothing shaky about it.

Yes. “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it?” I once told a hot batch to cool faster, and that batch ignored me completely. The writer's answer is right in the question: the Lord.
No king is named in this verse. The writer asks, “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it?” The name at the end is the Lord. That's the one who ordains it.
No elders in this verse either, friend. The question ends with the answer: “…unless the Lord has ordained it?” The name is the Lord. Nobody else is on the list.

Yes. “Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?” The writer puts adversity and good side by side in one question. I think that's him saying both out loud, with no tiptoeing.

Silence is in this poem, friend, but not in this verse. The writer asks, “Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?” Good is the word that fits the blank. It sits right beside adversity.

Fear is a fair guess when adversity is on the table, but the writer pairs it with something else. He asks, “Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?” Good is the word in the blank. Adversity and good, side by side.

Yes. The writer asks, “Why should any mortal man complain, in view of his sins?” It's a sober question, and I think it's meant to be read slowly. He asks it in the same poem that says the mercies are new every morning.
Wealth? Friend, the Millers bought me for a quarter, and even I know that's not the answer. The writer asks, “Why should any mortal man complain, in view of his sins?” Wealth never comes up.

Strength is a natural guess, but the writer doesn't say it. He asks, “Why should any mortal man complain, in view of his sins?” That's the answer. My own strength is a mustache, so I'd lose that argument anyway.
